entries.title: BACKDOOR
entries.body:
A *backdoor* is a secret mechanism that provides privileged access to a computer system, software, a function, an algorithm or data, without going through the usual authentication or security procedures. Unlike a security flaw, backdoors are intentionally introduced into the source code by malicious developers. They can be used to spy on, manipulate or steal sensitive information.

*The term "porte dérobée" is rarely used in French. The English term "backdoor" is generally preferred.*

entries.title: BINARY PREFIXES
entries.body: Units used in computing to quantify multiples of data sizes based on powers of 2. Unlike metric system prefixes, which use a base of 10, binary prefixes, such as kibi (Ki), mebi (Mi), gibi (Gi), and tebi (Ti), multiply by powers of 2 (`2^{10}`, `2^{20}`, `2^{30}`, `2^{40}` respectively). These prefixes are inherited from the earliest ways of measuring the size of information on computers. They are sometimes found in Bitcoin, for example to designate the size limit of the `BLOCKS/BLK*.DAT` files that store the raw blockchain data in the Bitcoin Core software. These files thus have a maximum capacity of 128 mebibytes (MiB), which is equivalent to a little over 134 megabytes (MB).

entries.title: BYZANTINE FAULT
entries.body:
A Byzantine fault, or Byzantine behavior, is any behavior of a system that does not comply with its own specifications, producing non-conforming results.

“Natural Byzantine faults” are commonly distinguished from “deliberate Byzantine faults”: the former generally stem from undetected physical errors (memory, network transmissions, etc.), while the latter mainly result from attacks aimed at making the system fail (sabotage, malicious intent, backdoor).

Authentication, signatures, and consensus by cryptographic means and “Byzantine Fault Tolerant” or “*Byzantine Fault Tolerant* (BFT)” algorithms make it possible to limit the latter.

*The Byzantine fault refers to the Byzantine Generals Problem, a metaphor dealing with the questioning of the reliability of transmissions and the integrity of the parties communicating.*

entries.title: BYZANTINE GENERALS PROBLEM
entries.body:
A problem first formulated by Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak and Marshall Pease in the specialized journal *ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems, vol 4, no. 3* [“The Byzantine Generals Problem”](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/byz.pdf) in July 1982. It is used today to illustrate the challenges of decision-making when a distributed system cannot trust any actor.

In this metaphor, a group of Byzantine generals and their respective armies are camped around a city that they wish to attack or besiege. The generals are geographically separated from one another and must communicate by messenger to coordinate their strategy. Whether they attack or retreat does not matter, as long as all the generals reach a consensus. 

We can therefore consider the following requirements:
* Each general must make a decision: attack or retreat (yes or no);
* Once the decision is made, it can no longer be changed;
* All generals must agree on the same decision and carry it out in a synchronized manner.

Furthermore, a general can communicate with another only through messages carried by a courier, which may be delayed, destroyed, altered or lost. And even if a message manages to be delivered, one or more generals may choose (for whatever reason) to betray the established trust, send a fraudulent message, and sow chaos.

If we apply the dilemma to the context of the Bitcoin blockchain, each general represents a node of the network, which must reach a consensus on the state of the system. In other words, the majority of the participants in a distributed network must agree and carry out the same action in order to avoid a total failure. The only way to reach a consensus in this type of distributed system is to have more than 2/3 of the network nodes be reliable and honest. Therefore, if the majority of the network decides to act maliciously, the system is vulnerable.

*This dilemma is sometimes also called the “Consistent Broadcast Problem”.*

entries.title: COINJOIN POOL
entries.body: In the context of coinjoins, a pool is a group of users who agree to mix their UTXOs uniformly in order to break their histories. A coinjoin pool imposes a fixed amount for the participating UTXOs, which guarantees that the inputs and outputs of the coinjoin transactions are identical, and thus prevents a link from being made between them. The more participants there are in a pool, the larger the anonsets the coins can gain there by going through several remix cycles.

entries.title: DEPTH
entries.body:
In the context of HD (hierarchical deterministic) wallets, depth designates the specific level of a key (public or private), a chain code, an extended key or an address in the wallet's derivation structure from the master key. Each level of this structure can be seen as a floor in a tree of keys, where the master key is at the root (depth 0) and the subsequent levels define various attributes such as:
the purpose (depth 1), the coin type (depth 2), the account (depth 3), the chain type (depth 4), and the index of the specific address (depth 5). 

![BIP-84 tree with its six depths: 0 master key, 1 purpose, 2 coin type, 3 account, 4 chain, 5 address.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/profondeur/assets/image-1.png)

To go from one depth to the next, a derivation process is used from a parent key pair to a child key pair.

*One also sometimes speaks of a “derivation level” rather than depth.*

entries.title: ENTRY POINT
entries.body:
Information that makes it possible to link an *on-chain* activity (an address, a transaction, a *cluster*...) to a form of identity belonging to a user or an entity. For example, if you publish your receiving address on Twitter under your name, an analyst could find it and associate it with your identity. In this case, the tweet would constitute an entry point for a chain analysis. To identify an entry point, analysts can use OSINT, but the most common method for associating an *on-chain* activity with an identity remains KYC.

![OSINT entry point: a public address on Twitter links Loïc's identity to the observed address cluster.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/point-d-entree/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: GENERATOR POINT
entries.body:
Fixed point on an elliptic curve that serves as the basis for all public-key cryptography operations. In Bitcoin, the generator point `G` is a standard parameter of the secp256k1 curve, defined deterministically. All Bitcoin users share the same generator point `G`. It is a public and universal parameter of the secp256k1 curve. Its coordinates are:

```
x=0x79BE667EF9DCBBAC55A06295CE870B07029BFCDB2DCE28D959F2815B16F81798
y=0x483ADA7726A3C4655DA4FBFC0E1108A8FD17B448A68554199C47D08FFB10D4B8
```

The generator point is the basis of public key derivation: a private key `k` (an integer) is associated with a public key `K` by scalar multiplication on the elliptic curve: `K = k * G`. This operation is easy to compute in one direction, but practically impossible to invert (the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves).

entries.title: HOT WALLET / SOFTWARE WALLET
entries.body: A hot wallet is a software device dedicated to securing and managing the private keys of a Bitcoin wallet. A wallet is called a hot wallet when the recovery phrase of a Bitcoin wallet is kept on a computing device, via software, that is not dedicated solely to Bitcoin use and that is directly connected to the internet. For example, a Bitcoin wallet application installed on your smartphone would be considered a hot wallet.

entries.title: INBOUND PEER / INCOMING CONNECTION
entries.body: Node on the Bitcoin network that initiates a connection to your node without any action on your part. Bitcoin Core allows a maximum of 114 inbound peers by default (out of a total of 125 connections), in order to facilitate connectivity within the network. Inbound peers are treated with caution, because there is no way to be sure they are honest, since they are initiated by third parties. Inbound and outbound peers share the same type of information. The main difference between inbound and outbound peers lies not in the type of information exchanged, but in the way these connections are established.

entries.title: MATURITY PERIOD
entries.body: The waiting period required before a block reward becomes spendable by the miner who received it. This period is set at 100 blocks following the mined block, i.e. 101 confirmations for the coinbase transaction. During this time, the bitcoins newly created in the block reward are not spendable. The purpose of this rule is to avoid the complications linked to the use of bitcoins coming from a chain that could later be made obsolete. Indeed, valid blocks sometimes end up being invalidated if another block, at the same height, is integrated into a chain benefiting from more work. This phenomenon, called a reorganization, results in the creation of an "orphan block" or "stale block," thus depriving the miner of the bitcoins contained in the coinbase of the abandoned block. If newly created bitcoins were immediately spendable, any transaction involving them could be cancelled after the fact, causing losses for the holders of those bitcoins. Such a scenario could lead to serial cancellations of otherwise valid transactions, thus affecting all users involved in this chain of transactions. The maturity period is therefore a mechanism to prevent this risk. By imposing a delay of 100 blocks before newly issued bitcoins can be used, we prevent coins from blocks that are ultimately invalidated from disrupting the system by circulating and affecting other transactions. The probability of a 101-block reorganization occurring is so low that it is considered nil.

entries.title: MEMPOOL POLICY
entries.body:
Subset of transaction relay policy that groups together the set of rules applied by a Bitcoin node to determine which unconfirmed transactions it accepts into its mempool. Mempool policy encompasses the standardness rules, but extends beyond them by including rules that take into account the context of the mempool as a whole, and not only the format of individual transactions.

For example, the rules relating to the minimum relay fee rate (`minRelayTxFee`), the maximum size of the mempool (`maxmempool`), or the transaction replacement rules (RBF) fall under mempool policy. These rules are configured locally by each node and may vary from one node to another.

Mempool policy is distinguished from standardness rules in that the latter concern only the format of a transaction taken in isolation, whereas mempool policy takes into account contextual factors such as mempool congestion, relationships between transactions, or the fee thresholds configured by the node operator.

entries.title: MEMPOOL PURGE
entries.body:
An event during which a Bitcoin node removes some of the pending transactions from its mempool. Each node maintains in memory a set of unconfirmed transactions, but this space is limited by resource constraints and by local policy rules. When certain conditions are met, the node performs a purge to free up space.

The most common cause is exceeding the maximum size allowed for the mempool. In Bitcoin Core, this limit is set by default to 300 MB via the parameter `maxmempool`. When this threshold is reached, the transactions that offer the lowest fee rate are evicted first in order to keep only those most likely to be included in an upcoming block. A transaction can also be purged if it remains pending too long without being confirmed. By default, this expiration period is 336 hours, or 14 days, via the parameter `mempoolexpiry`.

A purged transaction is not permanently canceled. It can be rebroadcast on the network by its sender or by another node that still holds it in its own mempool. The purge is a local resource management mechanism, and not a definitive rejection by the protocol.

entries.title: MNEMONIC PHRASE
entries.body:
A recovery phrase, also sometimes called a mnemonic, *seed phrase*, or secret phrase, is a sequence usually made up of 12 or 24 words, generated pseudo-randomly from a source of entropy. The pseudo-random sequence is always completed with a checksum (*checksum*). The mnemonic phrase, together with an optional passphrase, is used to deterministically derive all the keys associated with an HD (hierarchical deterministic) wallet. This means that from this phrase, it is possible to deterministically generate and recreate all the private and public keys of the Bitcoin wallet, and consequently to access the funds associated with it. The purpose of the recovery phrase is to provide a means of backing up and recovering bitcoins that is both secure and easy to use.

It is important to keep this phrase in a safe place and in a secure manner, because anyone in possession of the mnemonic would have access to the funds of the corresponding wallet. If it is used in a classic wallet, and without an optional passphrase, it is often a *SPOF* (single point of failure). The recovery phrase is therefore an encoding of the pseudo-random sequence and the *checksum* into everyday words in order to make it easier for humans to write down and read. It is built according to the BIP-0039 standard, which defines and orders a list of 2048 words used for this encoding.

*The list of 2048 words of BIP-0039 is available in several languages; however, it is advisable to use only the English version, because it is the version most widely supported by wallet software.*

entries.title: ORANGE PILL
entries.body:
Inspired by the film *Matrix*, this imaginary pill awakens one to the awareness of Bitcoin. 

*Also used as a verb. To orange-pill someone = to enlist them into Bitcoin.*

entries.title: OUTBOUND PEER / OUTGOING CONNECTION
entries.body: Node to which your own Bitcoin node actively establishes a connection. By default, a node attempts to connect to 8 outbound peers. These connections are preferred and considered more reliable than inbound peers, because they are chosen by the node. Inbound and outbound peers share the same type of information. The main difference between inbound and outbound peers lies not in the type of information exchanged, but in the way these connections are established.

entries.title: P2MS
entries.body:
P2MS is the acronym for *Pay to Multisig* (meaning “pay to multiple signatures”). It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. It allows bitcoins to be locked using several public keys. To spend these bitcoins, a signature must be provided with a predefined number of the associated private keys. For example, a `P2MS 2/3` has `3` public keys with `3` associated secret private keys. To spend the bitcoins locked with this P2MS script, a signature must be made with at least `2` of the `3` private keys. It is a threshold (*threshold*) security system.

This script was standardized in 2011 by Gavin Andresen, with the publication of BIP-0011, when he had just taken over maintenance of Bitcoin's main client. The opcode `OP_CHECKMULTISIG`, on which it relies, already existed in Bitcoin's original source code, but scripts that used it were not standard before this proposal. Today, P2MS is only marginally used by some applications. The vast majority of modern multisignatures use other scripts such as P2SH, P2WSH or P2TR. Compared to these, P2MS is extremely trivial. The public keys that make it up are revealed as soon as the transaction is received. Using a P2MS is also more expensive than the other multisignature scripts.

*P2MS scripts are often called “bare-multisig”, which can be translated as “naked multisignatures”, or “raw multisignatures”. In early 2023, P2MS scripts were at the center of a controversy because of their misuse within the Stamps protocol. Their impact on the UTXO set was notably singled out.*

entries.title: P2P - PEER-TO-PEER
entries.body:
Refers to a model of communication and data distribution in which participants, often called nodes or peers, share their resources (such as files, processing power, bandwidth, assets…) directly with each other, without requiring a centralized intermediary. In a P2P system, each participant acts simultaneously as a client (consumer of resources) and as a server (provider of resources).

The Bitcoin system operates according to a P2P model, where nodes are responsible for validating transactions and storing the blockchain. This means that, unlike traditional banking systems which depend on centralized entities, Bitcoin operates on a distributed structure where no single entity holds control. The nodes of the Bitcoin network communicate with each other to broadcast transactions and blocks, and to reach consensus on the state of the ledger.

entries.title: P2P TRANSPORT V2
entries.body:
New version of the Bitcoin P2P transport protocol integrating opportunistic encryption to improve the privacy and security of communications between nodes. This improvement aims to address several problems of the base version of the P2P protocol, notably by making the exchanged data indistinguishable to a passive observer (such as an internet service provider), thereby reducing the risks of censorship and of attacks based on detecting specific patterns in data packets.

The encryption put in place does not include authentication, so as not to add unnecessary complexity and not to compromise the fact that connecting to the network remains permissionless. This new P2P transport protocol nonetheless offers better security against passive attacks and makes active attacks (notably MITM attacks) significantly more costly and detectable. The introduction of a pseudo-random data stream complicates the task of attackers wishing to censor or manipulate communications.

P2P transport V2 was included as an option (disabled by default) in version 26.0 of Bitcoin Core, released in December 2023. It can be enabled with the option `v2transport=1` in the configuration file.

entries.title: P2PK
entries.body:
P2PK is the acronym for *Pay to Public Key*. It is a standard script template used on Bitcoin to set spending conditions on a UTXO. It allows bitcoins to be locked directly to a public key, rather than to an address.
Technically, the P2PK script contains a public key and an instruction that requires a matching digital signature to unlock the funds. When the owner wishes to spend the bitcoins, they must provide a signature produced with the associated private key. This signature is verified with the ECDSA algorithm (*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*). P2PK was often used in the early versions of Bitcoin, notably by Satoshi Nakamoto. It is almost no longer used today.

entries.title: P2PKH
entries.body:
P2PKH is the acronym for *Pay to Public Key Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. It allows bitcoins to be locked to a hash of a public key, that is, to a receiving address. This script is associated with the Legacy standard, and was introduced in the earliest versions of Bitcoin by Satoshi Nakamoto.

Unlike P2PK, where the public key is explicitly included in the script, P2PKH relies on a cryptographic fingerprint of the public key. This script includes the `RIPEMD160` hash of the `SHA256` of the public key and stipulates that, to access the funds, the recipient must provide a public key matching this hash, as well as a valid digital signature generated from the associated private key. P2PKH addresses are encoded using the `Base58Check` format, which gives them robustness against typographical errors through the use of a checksum. These addresses always begin with the digit `1`.

entries.title: P2POOL
entries.body:
Decentralized mining pool protocol for Bitcoin, designed to eliminate the need for a central operator. P2Pool works by creating a secondary blockchain called the “share chain”, whose difficulty is adjusted to produce a block approximately every 30 seconds. The blocks of this *share chain* are structurally identical to those of the Bitcoin blockchain, but with a lower difficulty target. Each miner runs their own P2Pool node connected to a Bitcoin full node and contributes to the peer-to-peer network of the *share chain*.

When one of the blocks of the *share chain* also satisfies the difficulty required by the Bitcoin network, it is broadcast on the Bitcoin network. The block reward is then distributed among the miners who contributed the most recent shares in the *share chain*. This mechanism ensures that the distribution of rewards is proportional to each miner's contribution, without a central operator controlling the funds or the selection of transactions.

P2Pool was created in 2011 by Forrest Voight. It saw significant adoption in the early years of Bitcoin, but its use declined in the face of the growth of centralized pools, which offered simpler interfaces and lower variance for individual miners. The last block mined by P2Pool dates from 2019.

entries.title: P2SH
entries.body:
P2SH is the acronym for *Pay to Script Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. Unlike the P2PK and P2PKH scripts, where the spending conditions are predefined, P2SH allows the integration of arbitrary spending conditions and additional functionality within a transaction script.

Technically, in a P2SH transaction, the `scriptPubKey` contains the cryptographic fingerprint of a `redeemScript`, rather than explicit spending conditions. This fingerprint is obtained using a `HASH160` hash, that is, a `SHA256` followed by a `RIPEMD160`. When sending bitcoins to a P2SH address, the underlying `redeemScript` is not revealed. Only its fingerprint is included in the transaction. P2SH addresses are encoded in `Base58Check` and begin with the digit `3`. When the recipient wishes to spend the bitcoins received, they must provide a `redeemScript` matching the fingerprint present in the `scriptPubKey`, as well as the data needed to satisfy the conditions of this `redeemScript`. For example, in a multisignature P2SH, the script could require signatures from several private keys.

Using P2SH gives more flexibility, as it allows the construction of arbitrary scripts without the sender knowing their details. P2SH was introduced in 2012 with BIP-0016.

entries.title: P2SH-P2WPKH
entries.body:
P2SH-P2WPKH is the acronym for *Pay to Script Hash - Pay to Witness Public Key Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO, also known as “Nested SegWit”.

P2SH-P2WPKH was introduced with the implementation of SegWit in August 2017. This script is a P2WPKH wrapped within a P2SH. It locks bitcoins based on the hash of a public key. The difference from the standard P2WPKH is that the script is here wrapped in the `redeemScript` of a standard P2SH.

This script was created at the launch of SegWit to facilitate its adoption. It makes it possible to use this new standard, even with services or *wallets* not yet natively compatible with SegWit. It is a sort of transition script toward the new standard. Today, it is therefore no longer very relevant to use this type of *wrapped* SegWit scripts, since most *wallets* have implemented native SegWit. P2SH-P2WPKH addresses are written using the `Base58Check` encoding and always begin with `3`, like any P2SH address.

*`P2SH-P2WPKH` is also sometimes called `P2WPKH-nested-in-P2SH`.*

entries.title: P2SH-P2WSH
entries.body:
P2SH-P2WSH is the acronym for *Pay to Script Hash - Pay to Witness Script Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO, also known as “*Nested SegWit*”.

P2SH-P2WSH was introduced with the implementation of SegWit in August 2017. This script describes a P2WSH wrapped within a P2SH. It locks bitcoins based on the hash of a script. The difference from the standard P2WSH is that the script is wrapped in the `redeemScript` of a standard P2SH.

This script was created at the launch of SegWit to facilitate its adoption. It makes it possible to use this new standard, even with services or *wallets* not yet natively compatible with SegWit. Today, it is therefore no longer very relevant to use this type of *wrapped* SegWit scripts, since most *wallets* have implemented native SegWit. P2SH-P2WSH addresses are written using the `Base58Check` encoding and always begin with `3`, like any P2SH address.

entries.title: P2TR
entries.body:
P2TR is the acronym for *Pay to Taproot*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. It was introduced with the implementation of Taproot in November 2021. P2TR uses the Schnorr protocol to aggregate cryptographic keys, as well as Merkle trees for alternative scripts, known as MAST (*Merkelized Alternative Script Tree*). Unlike traditional transactions where the spending conditions are publicly exposed (sometimes at receipt, sometimes at spending), P2TR makes it possible to hide complex scripts behind a single apparent public key.

Technically, a P2TR script locks bitcoins to a single Schnorr public key, called `K`. However, this `K` key is actually an aggregate of a public key `P` and a public key `M`, the latter being computed from the Merkle root of a list of `scriptPubKey`. Bitcoins locked with a P2TR script can be spent in two distinct ways: either by publishing a signature for the public key `P`, or by satisfying one of the scripts contained in the Merkle tree. The first option is called the “*key path*” and the second the “*script path*”.

Thus, P2TR allows users to send bitcoins either to a public key, or to several scripts of their choice. Another advantage of this script is that, although there are multiple ways to spend a P2TR output, only the one that is used must be revealed at spending, allowing the unused alternatives to remain private. P2TR is a version 1 SegWit output, which means that the signatures for P2TR inputs are stored in the witness of a transaction, and not in the `scriptSig`. P2TR addresses use a `Bech32m` encoding and begin with `bc1p`.

entries.title: P2WPKH
entries.body:
P2WPKH is the acronym for *Pay to Witness Public Key Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. P2WPKH was introduced with the implementation of SegWit in August 2017.

This script is similar to P2PKH (*Pay to Public Key Hash*), since it also locks bitcoins based on the hash of a public key, that is, of a receiving address. The difference lies in the way signatures and scripts are included in the transaction. Under P2WPKH, the signature script information (`scriptSig`) is moved from the traditional structure of the transaction to a separate section called `Witness` (witness). This move is a feature of the SegWit (*Segregated Witness*) update that makes it possible to prevent signature-related malleability. P2WPKH transactions are generally less costly in terms of fees compared to Legacy transactions, because the part in the witness costs less.

P2WPKH addresses are written using the `Bech32` encoding with a checksum in the form of a BCH code. These addresses always begin with `bc1q`. P2WPKH is a version 0 SegWit output.

entries.title: P2WSH
entries.body:
P2WSH is the acronym for *Pay to Witness Script Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. P2WSH was introduced with the implementation of SegWit in August 2017.

This script is similar to P2SH (*Pay to Script Hash*), since it also locks bitcoins based on the hash of a script. The difference lies in the way signatures and scripts are included in the transaction. To spend the bitcoins on this type of script, the beneficiary must provide the original script, called `witnessScript` (equivalent of the `redeemScript`), as well as the required signatures. This mechanism makes it possible to implement more sophisticated spending conditions, such as multisigs.

Under P2WSH, the signature script information (the `scriptWitness`, the equivalent of the `scriptSig`) is moved from the traditional structure of the transaction to a separate section called `Witness` (witness). This move is a feature of the SegWit (*Segregated Witness*) update that makes it possible to prevent signature-related malleability. P2WSH transactions are generally less costly in terms of fees compared to Legacy transactions, because the part in the witness costs less.

P2WSH addresses are written using the `Bech32` encoding with a checksum in the form of a BCH code. These addresses always begin with `bc1q`. P2WSH is a version 0 SegWit output.

entries.title: PACKAGE RELAY
entries.body:
Improvement to Bitcoin's relay protocol that allows nodes to transmit and evaluate groups of interdependent transactions collectively, rather than processing them individually. Without this mechanism, a parent transaction whose fee rate is too low to be accepted into the mempool is rejected, which prevents any child transaction from being used for CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*), since the parent is needed for its validation.

This problem is particularly critical for time-constrained protocols such as the Lightning Network, where transactions are signed well before they are broadcast. The minimum fee rate accepted by a node depends on the content of its mempool at a given moment; a parent transaction that was previously eligible for CPFP may therefore no longer be so at the time of its broadcast.

*Package relay* solves this problem by evaluating the combined fee rate of a parent-child set. The current implementation in Bitcoin Core focuses on a variant limited to one parent and one child (1p1c), which does not require a modification of the P2P protocol. BIP-0331 formalizes the more general specification of ancestor package relay. The main development challenge lies in preventing denial-of-service vulnerabilities.

This mechanism is complementary to *anchor outputs* and constitutes an important countermeasure against transaction pinning (*transaction pinning*) attacks.

entries.title: PAIRING PHRASE
entries.body: Sequence of words used by the Lightning Node Connect (LNC) protocol to authenticate and secure a remote connection to a Lightning node. The *pairing phrase* is generated by the node via *litd* and passed to the user, who enters it in Lightning Terminal or any other compatible application. It establishes an end-to-end encrypted channel through a proxy server, without requiring a VPN, port forwarding, or direct exposure of the node to the internet.

entries.title: PAPER WALLET
entries.body: Offline storage method that consists of printing or writing down a pair of cryptographic keys giving access to bitcoins on paper (or possibly another physical medium) only. Paper wallets are considered a cold storage method, because they are not connected to the internet, provided they were produced manually and not printed. Their security then relies on the physical protection of the paper against loss, destruction, and theft. They are now often considered obsolete, because they offer a weaker security model than modern solutions. Moreover, their use often involves reusing the same public key, which is very problematic for the user's privacy.

entries.title: PASSIVE ASSETS
entries.body: In the Taproot Assets protocol, passive assets refer to the assets that the sender keeps in their asset tree (*asset tree*) when making a transfer. When sending, the tree is modified: the assets actively transferred to a new holder are called “active”, while those that remain in the sender's possession are called “passive”. These passive assets must be re-anchored (*re-anchored*) in a new Merkle root to maintain the integrity of the tree after the transaction.

entries.title: PASSPHRASE - BIP-0039
entries.body:
Optional password that, combined with the recovery phrase, provides an additional layer of security for deterministic and hierarchical Bitcoin wallets. HD wallets are generally generated from a recovery phrase made up of 12 or 24 words. This recovery phrase is very important, because it makes it possible to restore all of a wallet's keys in case of loss. However, it is a single point of failure (SPOF). If it is compromised, the bitcoins are at risk. This is where the passphrase comes in. It is an optional password, chosen by the user, that is added to the recovery phrase to strengthen the wallet's security. Not to be confused with a PIN code or an ordinary password, the passphrase plays a role in the derivation of the cryptographic keys. 

It works in tandem with the recovery phrase, modifying the seed from which the keys are generated. Thus, even if someone obtains your recovery phrase, without the passphrase they cannot access your funds. Using a passphrase essentially creates a new wallet with distinct keys. Changing the passphrase (even slightly) will generate a different wallet.

The passphrase is arbitrary and can be any combination of characters chosen by the user. Using a passphrase offers several advantages. First, it reduces the risks linked to the compromise of the recovery phrase by requiring a second factor to access the funds. Second, it can be used strategically to create decoy wallets containing small amounts of bitcoins, in the event of physical coercion to steal your funds. Finally, its use is valuable when you want to control the randomness of the generation of the HD wallet's seed. The passphrase must be complex enough to resist brute-force attacks and must be backed up reliably. Losing the passphrase can result in the inability to access the funds, just like losing the recovery phrase.

*The passphrase is sometimes also called: “two-factor seed phrase”, “password”, “seed extension”, “extension word”, or even “13th or 25th word”. Note that there are two types of passphrases on Bitcoin. The best known is the one described above, which depends on BIP-0039, and which makes it possible to secure an entire HD wallet. However, BIP-0038 had also specified a way to secure a single private key using a passphrase. This second type of passphrase is almost no longer used today.*

entries.title: PASSPORT
entries.body: *Hardware wallet* made by the American company Foundation Devices, designed exclusively for Bitcoin. The Passport is a fully *air-gapped* device that communicates with wallet software via a camera and QR codes, with no wired connection for signing transactions. It incorporates a *secure element* and its *firmware* is *open source*. The device has a color screen and a directional pad, and is powered by a removable lithium-ion battery in the Nokia BL-5C format. The Passport works with the Envoy companion app, as well as with third-party software such as Sparrow Wallet.

entries.title: PATHFINDING
entries.body:
Process used by a node to determine the optimal path to route a payment through the network of Lightning channels. *Pathfinding* is performed by the payer's node, which must select the most suitable intermediate nodes to reach the recipient. This choice is based on several criteria such as fees, channel capacity, and *timelocks*.

*Pathfinding* algorithms build a graph of the network topology from *gossip* data and evaluate the different possible routes between the paying node and the receiver. These routes are ranked from best to worst according to various criteria. The node then tries these routes until it succeeds in making the payment on one of them.

entries.title: PATOSHI
entries.body: Refers to a distinct pattern of nonces and timestamps observed in blocks mined during the first months of Bitcoin's existence. This pattern is suspected to be attributable to a single entity or individual, most likely Satoshi Nakamoto himself, the inventor of Bitcoin. The term “Patoshi” is a portmanteau combining “*pattern*” and “Satoshi”. Several analyses of Bitcoin's first blocks revealed patterns in the way nonces and extra-nonces were chosen, and in how timestamps were set. These patterns were distinct enough to suggest that a particular miner or group of miners was responsible for a large proportion of the blocks mined during this period, while using a modified client. Sergio Demian Lerner, a computer science researcher, is credited with discovering this pattern in 2013. Lerner estimated that the Patoshi miner had mined about 1.1 million bitcoins. This led to widespread speculation about the motivations, identity, and current intentions of the Patoshi miner. Some believe that Patoshi was Satoshi himself, mining bitcoins to support and secure the nascent network. It is important to note that, although the Patoshi pattern is widely accepted as evidence of concentrated early mining activity, there is no definitive confirmation of the identity behind Patoshi or of their intentions.

entries.title: PAY-TO-CONTRACT
entries.body:
Cryptographic protocol that makes it possible to commit arbitrary data into a Bitcoin public key, so that a payment made to this key simultaneously constitutes proof of commitment to that data.

The principle relies on “tweaking” a public key: from an original public key `P` and a contract `c`, a new key `P' = P + H(P \| c) \cdot G` is computed, where `H` is a hash function and `G` the generator point of the curve. The resulting key `P'` appears to be an ordinary public key, but it encodes a verifiable commitment to the contract `c`. The payer can then prove to a third party what they paid for, by revealing the original key `P` and the contract `c`, without this proof being visible on the blockchain.

entries.title: PAYJOIN
entries.body:
Specific Bitcoin transaction structure that improves users' privacy when spending by collaborating with the payment recipient. The distinctive feature of Payjoin is its ability to generate a transaction that looks ordinary at first glance, but is in reality a mini coinjoin between two people. To do this, the transaction structure involves the payment recipient in the inputs alongside the actual sender. The recipient therefore includes a payment to themselves in the middle of the transaction that itself serves to pay them. For example, if you buy a baguette for `6 000 sats` using a UTXO of `10 000 sats`, and you opt for a Payjoin, your baker will add a UTXO of `15 000 sats` belonging to them as an input, which they will recover in full as an output, in addition to your `6 000 sats`.

The Payjoin transaction fulfills two purposes. First, it aims to mislead an outside observer by creating a decoy in chain analysis based on the CIOH heuristic (*Common Input Ownership Heuristic*). Usually, when a transaction on the blockchain has several inputs, it is assumed that all these inputs likely belong to a single entity. Thus, when an analyst examines a Payjoin transaction, they are led to believe that all the inputs come from one person. However, this perception is wrong, because the payment recipient also contributes inputs alongside the actual payer. Second, Payjoin also makes it possible to deceive an outside observer about the actual amount of the payment that was made. By examining the structure of the transaction, the analyst might believe that the payment is equivalent to the amount of one of the outputs. In reality, the payment amount does not match any of the outputs. It is in fact the difference between the recipient's UTXO as an output and the recipient's UTXO as an input. In this respect, the Payjoin transaction falls within the domain of steganography. It makes it possible to hide the actual amount of a transaction within a fake transaction that acts as a decoy.

![Payjoin between a buyer and a baker: 2 inputs and 2 outputs mixed together, the actual payment of 6,000 sats remains hidden.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/payjoin/assets/image-1.png)

*Payjoin is also sometimes called “P2EP (Pay-to-End-Point)”, “Stowaway”, or “steganographic transaction”.*

entries.title: PAYMENT HASH
entries.body: Cryptographic fingerprint of the *preimage* used to secure a payment on the Lightning Network. When a recipient creates an *invoice*, they generate a random secret (the *preimage*), compute its hash, and embed it in the *invoice*. The sender then builds a chain of HTLCs locked by this hash along the payment route. The payment is finalized only when the recipient reveals the corresponding *preimage*, allowing each intermediate node to unlock its funds in turn.

entries.title: PAYNYM
entries.body:
Unique identifier linked to a Bitcoin wallet that implements this option. Paynyms are available on Samourai Wallet and on Sparrow Wallet. Originally, these identifiers are generated from the wallet's payment code, in accordance with BIP-0047. They thus offer the possibility of connecting with another user in order to generate fresh, unique receiving addresses, without requiring direct interaction. The use of Paynyms was later broadened to support various other features of the Samourai ecosystem. They are notably used to enable encrypted exchanges over the Soroban communication protocol, in order to easily carry out collaborative transactions. Paynyms can also be used for authentication on systems compatible with the AUTH47 protocol. Each Paynym is characterized by a unique identifier and is represented by an illustration of a robot.

![Three examples of Paynym robot illustrations, the visual avatar generated from the BIP-0047 payment code.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/paynym/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: PBKDF2
entries.body:
`PBKDF2` is the acronym for *Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2*. It is a method for creating cryptographic keys from a password using a derivation function. It takes as input a password and a cryptographic salt, and iteratively applies a predetermined function (often a hash function such as `SHA256` or a `HMAC`) to this data. This process is repeated many times in order to generate a cryptographic key. 

In the context of Bitcoin, `PBKDF2` is used in conjunction with the `HMAC-SHA512` function to create the seed of a deterministic and hierarchical wallet (seed) from a recovery phrase of 12 or 24 words. The cryptographic salt used in this case is the string `"mnemonic"` concatenated with the optional BIP-0039 passphrase, and the number of iterations is `2048`.

entries.title: PEACH
entries.body:
Peer-to-peer (P2P) bitcoin exchange mobile application, founded in 2022 in Switzerland. Peach Bitcoin, often simply called “Peach”, allows users to buy and sell bitcoins directly between themselves without going through a centralized exchange platform.

The application works with an *escrow* system to secure transactions and supports many payment methods in Europe, such as SEPA transfers, Revolut, PayPal, or cash payments at in-person meetings.

entries.title: PEDERSEN COMMITMENT
entries.body:
A Pedersen commitment is a type of cryptographic commitment with the property of being homomorphic with respect to the addition operation. This means it is possible to validate the sum of two commitments without revealing the individual values.

Formally, if:
```math
C_1\ =\ commit(m_1,\ r_1) \quad C_2\ =\ commit(m_2,\ r_2)
```
then:
```math
C_3\ =\ C_1 \cdot C_2\ =\ commit(m_1\ +\ m_2,\ r_1\ +\ r_2)
```
This property becomes useful, for example, to conceal the amounts of *tokens* exchanged in cryptocurrency systems, such as RGB, while still being able to verify the totals.

entries.title: PEELING CHAIN
entries.body:
Transaction pattern on the blockchain in which a large amount of bitcoins is gradually distributed through a long series of successive transactions. At each step, a fraction is sent to a recipient, while the remainder goes back to a new change address. The residual balance thus decreases from transaction to transaction: each amount is “peeled” (*peeled*) from the remaining total. The chain can extend over hundreds, even thousands of transactions.

This pattern is characteristic of automated withdrawals from exchange platforms, mining pools, or payment services, but it is also used for money laundering, because the small individual amounts attract less attention from compliance systems.

In chain analysis, the *peeling chain* is an easy pattern to identify, because each transaction generally has only one input and two outputs with very asymmetric amounts. Identifying it makes it possible to follow the thread of payments and reconstruct the flows of funds from a single source.

entries.title: PEER DISCOVERY
PEERS.DAT
entries.body:
File in which Bitcoin Core serializes the tables of the `addrman` module: the "new" table (addresses that have been discovered but not yet tested) and the "tried" table (addresses to which the node has already connected successfully). It contains the IP addresses of the other nodes, port numbers, last-connection timestamps, and the bucketing key (`nKey`) that determines the placement of addresses in the buckets.

On first launch, the file does not exist and the tables are empty: the node queries the DNS seeds to obtain an initial list of peers. As connections are made, addresses are inserted into the tables and `peers.dat` is periodically updated. It is also possible to add addresses manually via the `-addnode` option or the `addnode` RPC command.

This file replaced `addr.dat` starting with Bitcoin Core 0.7.0 (2012), when Pieter Wuille introduced `addrman` with its deterministic bucketing system.

entries.title: PEG-IN
entries.body:
Mechanism by which the value of bitcoins is transferred from the main blockchain to a sidechain. The process consists of locking BTC on the main chain by sending them to a special address managed by a trusted third party or a group, or to a script that makes them temporarily unusable, and then issuing an equivalent quantity of tokens on the sidechain. This locking guarantees that the bitcoins cannot be spent simultaneously on both chains. Once the peg-in is done, the user can make use of the features specific to the sidechain. The peg-in is the first step of the two-way peg (*two-way peg*) that links the main chain to the sidechain.

As an individual, it is generally not necessary to use a peg-in, since there are *atomic swap* systems that make it possible to exchange *onchain* bitcoins for bitcoins on Liquid (or on another sidechain, as applicable).

entries.title: PEG-OUT
entries.body: The reverse mechanism of the peg-in, by which tokens circulating on a sidechain are destroyed in order to release the corresponding bitcoins on the main blockchain. The user initiates the process by sending their tokens to a burn address on the sidechain, which triggers the unlocking of the BTC previously locked on the main chain. The peg-out is the second step of the two-way peg (*two-way peg*) and makes it possible to return to the Bitcoin blockchain at any time. Depending on the implementation, this process may be handled by a federation of signers, as is the case on Liquid, or in an automated way via cryptographic proofs.

entries.title: PERCOLATION
entries.body: Refers to a model for understanding the spread of information (transactions and blocks) across the network of Bitcoin nodes. Percolation theory is originally a mathematical and physical model that studies the movement and filtration of fluids through porous materials. It analyzes how, beyond a certain threshold, a connected network allows the fluid to flow continuously through the material. It can be applied to computer networks to see how information spreads, by considering nodes as sites that can be either active or inactive. In Bitcoin, nodes thus play the role of the pores in percolation theory. Each active node receives and transmits the information to other nodes, which will either continue the transmission or block it. The propagation of certain types of transactions can be analyzed in terms of percolation thresholds, where a certain percentage of active nodes is needed to reach a miner who will include it in a block. This theory provides a framework for evaluating how changes in the network, such as certain nodes modifying their standardness rules, affect the cascading propagation mechanism of transactions to reach a miner.

entries.title: PHOENIX
entries.body: *Self-custodial* mobile wallet software designed to simplify transactions on the Lightning protocol and make them more accessible. It allows users to manage their funds directly from their mobile devices without needing to connect to a separate Lightning node. Phoenix in fact works as a genuine standalone Lightning node on the phone (*lightning-kmp* implementation). It supports Bitcoin and Lightning transactions, and offers features to ease node management, such as automatic channel management with Acinq's node. Unlike other Lightning wallet applications, which are mostly custodial, Phoenix offers an interesting compromise by combining the use of a Lightning node with the convenience of a smartphone application. It is one of the best solutions that is simple to get started with for a beginner who wants to use Lightning while keeping full possession of their bitcoins (*self-custody*). Phoenix is a project developed and maintained by the French company Acinq.

entries.title: PHOENIXD
entries.body: Specialized implementation of a Lightning node, designed to send and receive payments from a server. Phoenixd uses the same software as the Phoenix mobile wallet/node, but unlike the latter, which is exclusively intended for smartphones, phoenixd is able to run on a server as a *daemon*. Instead of having a graphical user interface (GUI), it is equipped with an HTTP API interface and handles automatic management of channels and liquidity. Phoenixd is a project developed and maintained by the French company ACINQ.

entries.title: PIZZA DAY
entries.body: Event celebrated every May 22 by the Bitcoin community that commemorates the first transaction of bitcoins for a physical good. In 2010, Laszlo Hanyecz, a Bitcoin developer, [proposed on the BitcoinTalk forum](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=137.msg1141#msg1141) to buy two large pizzas for 10,000 BTC, then equivalent to about 40 dollars. On May 22, he confirmed that the offer had been accepted by a 19-year-old Californian student, Jeremy Sturdivant, known under the pseudonym Jercos. He ordered the pizzas from Papa John's and had them delivered to Laszlo in Florida. This day marks an important moment for Bitcoin since it demonstrates its potential as a medium of exchange. Every year, the community celebrates this event by eating pizzas paid for in bitcoins.

entries.title: POLAR
entries.body: Local simulation tool for the Lightning Network intended for development and testing. Developed by Jamal James, Polar makes it possible to quickly create a complete Lightning network on your computer, with several interconnected LND, CLN or Eclair nodes, without needing real bitcoins or a connection to the Bitcoin network. The graphical interface makes it possible to visualize channels, send test payments, and simulate different routing scenarios, which makes it a valuable tool for developers of Lightning applications.

entries.title: POLICY - MINISCRIPT
entries.body:
High-level, user-oriented language for simply specifying conditions under which a UTXO can be unlocked within the framework of Miniscript. The *policy* is an abstract description of the spending rules. It can then be compiled into miniscript, which is one-to-one equivalent to operations of Bitcoin's native script language. 

![Miniscript pipeline: the readable policy compiles into miniscript, which is then translated into native Bitcoin script.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/policy-miniscript/assets/image-1.png)

The *policy* language is slightly different from the miniscript language. For example, imagine a security system with key A on the primary path, and key B on the recovery path, but under a one-year *timelock* (about 52,560 blocks). In *policy*, this would give:

```plaintext
or(pk(A),and(pk(B),older(52560)))
```

Once compiled into miniscript, it would give: 

```plaintext
andor(pk(B),older(52560),pk(A))
```

And once converted into native script, it would give:

```plaintext
<B>
OP_CHECKSIG
OP_NOTIF
<A>
OP_CHECKSIG
OP_ELSE
<50cd00>
OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY
OP_ENDIF
```

entries.title: POOL - LIGHTNING
entries.body: Service developed by Lightning Labs. It is a kind of marketplace for liquidity in Lightning channels. Pool connects users who need access to liquidity on LN with those who have capital to deploy on the network​​. Participants can earn satoshis by opening new channels for those looking to receive funds on Lightning for a set period of time​​. Pool also makes it possible to rent a channel in order to instantly accept Bitcoin payments.

entries.title: POOL HOPPING
entries.body: Refers to the practice of some miners who frequently switch mining pools in order to maximize their earnings. These miners move from one pool to another depending on variations in profitability. This strategy exploits the differences in the pools' reward calculation methods. *Pool hopping* can unbalance the distribution of rewards within pools and is generally considered an unfair practice in the community.

entries.title: PORTAL
entries.body: *Open source* Bitcoin *hardware wallet* developed by TwentyTwo Devices, which works entirely via NFC, with no cable or battery. The device is powered directly by the *smartphone*'s NFC field. Its *firmware* is written in Rust with BDK (*Bitcoin Dev Kit*) and it is compatible with mobile wallets such as Nunchuk or Bitcoin Keeper for signing transactions.

entries.title: POSTMIX
entries.body:
Account that groups the UTXOs that have participated in at least one coinjoin cycle in the Whirlpool protocol. The postmix represents the mixed funds whose link to their origin has been broken thanks to the coinjoin process.

UTXOs in the postmix account benefit from anonsets that increase with each additional coinjoin cycle. The more a UTXO participates in remixes (which are free in Whirlpool), the more its forward-looking and backward-looking anonymity set grows, which strengthens its privacy.

Using postmix UTXOs requires particular care so as not to degrade the privacy gained. Merging postmix UTXOs with each other or with unmixed UTXOs can re-establish traceable links. Spends from the postmix are best made using privacy-preserving techniques, such as Stonewall or Stonewall x2.

entries.title: POT - PAY ON TARGET
entries.body: Method for calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools. POT is a compensation system that varies according to the difficulty of the work sent to the pool rather than that of the work provided by the pool. In this approach, the reward for each share submitted by a miner is based on the difficulty of that specific share. This means that more difficult shares are better rewarded than less difficult ones. It is a variant of PPS, but by adjusting the reward according to the actual complexity of the work accomplished, POT involves much more variance for the miner.

entries.title: POW - PROOF OF WORK
entries.body:
A protection mechanism against Sybil attacks, which are characterized by the multiplication of fake identities in order to gain an illegitimate advantage. Proof of work thus establishes a significant marginal cost for multiplying votes on Bitcoin. Proof of work is the foundation of Nakamoto consensus, which is the principle used to establish agreement on a single version of the ledger distributed among the various nodes of the network. Concretely, proof of work is the search for a value that, once passed through a random mathematical function, gives a result less than or equal to a target number. This proof-of-work target is adjusted every 2016 blocks by the nodes. This is what is called the difficulty adjustment. The target number is lowered to increase the mining difficulty, or raised to decrease the difficulty, depending on how the computing power deployed by miners changed over the previous period. 

![Proof of work: hashing the header with SHA256d until obtaining a hash that falls below the difficulty target.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/preuve-de-travail/assets/image-1.png)

This work performed by miners is rewarded for each valid block found. The winning miner collects a monetary reward, made up of the block subsidy (the creation of new bitcoins ex nihilo) and transaction fees. Today, the difficulty of proof of work on Bitcoin is such that mining requires a great deal of computing power to succeed in winning blocks. As a result, it is often necessary to have electronic chips specialized in running `SHA256d`, called ASICs, and to take part in mining pools.

entries.title: PPA
entries.body: Acronym for "*Power Purchase Agreement*". It is a long-term contract between a large bitcoin mining farm and an energy provider, for the direct purchase of electricity at a fixed rate. This type of contract allows mining farms to secure stable and competitive energy costs over several years, which reduces the impact of fluctuations in the electricity market.

entries.title: PPLNS - PAY PER LAST N SHARES
entries.french: PPLNS - PAY PER LAST N SHARES
entries.body: Method for calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools. PPLNS rewards miners based on their contribution in *shares* over a given period. In PPLNS, payments are made only when the pool finds a block and are based on the number of *shares* submitted by the miner relative to the total *shares* collected during the observed period. This method favors consistent miners who are active over the long term, because it discourages *pool hopping* (frequently switching pools). The compensation varies with the probability of finding a block, which can lead to lower consistency in the miner's income (more variance than pay-per-task).

entries.title: PPS - PAY PER SHARE
entries.body:
Method for calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools. PPS is a system in which miners are paid for each valid share submitted, regardless of whether or not the pool finds a block. They are therefore paid on the expected value. It is a pay-per-task compensation method. 

Each submitted share is considered a contribution to the mining process and has a predetermined fixed value. This method offers stable and predictable compensation for miners, because it eliminates the variance linked to the probability of finding a block. However, it is riskier for pool operators, because they must pay miners even when no block is found, thereby absorbing the variance risk. Unlike the FPPS method, PPS does not include transaction fees in the calculation of compensation.

entries.title: PPS+
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Pay Per Share Plus*". Method for calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools, which combines the PPS and PPLNS approaches. For the portion related to the block subsidy, miners receive fixed compensation for each valid *share* submitted, calculated according to the classic PPS method, regardless of whether the pool found a block or not. For the portion related to transaction fees, the compensation is distributed according to the PPLNS method, only when a block is actually found by the pool.

PPS+ thus offers miners a stable income base thanks to the PPS component, while allowing them to benefit from transaction fees when the pool finds a block. This method is less risky for the pool operator than FPPS, because the operator does not advance the transaction fees.

seeAlso.title: PPLNS - PAY PER LAST N SHARES

entries.title: PRAXEOLOGY
entries.body:
General science of human action, developed by Ludwig von Mises within the framework of the Austrian School of economics. Praxeology studies intentional, goal-directed behavior. It rests on a fundamental axiom: the individual acts deliberately to move from a state they judge less satisfactory to a state they perceive as better. This axiom is considered irrefutable, because any attempt to contradict it is itself an action, which validates it. Economics, as catallactics, is a branch of praxeology.

The praxeological method is axiomatic and deductive: it starts from propositions considered true a priori in order to logically deduce economic laws from them, without resorting to empirical experimentation or econometrics. This approach is radically distinct from the positivism of other economic schools of thought. It implies, in particular, that prices, money and economic cycles are analyzed as phenomena emerging from individual action, and not as statistical aggregates.

In the Bitcoin ecosystem, praxeology is often invoked to analyze bitcoin as an emergent money, whose adoption and value stem from the voluntary choices of individuals acting in their own interest, without central planning.

entries.title: PREIMAGE
entries.body:
In mathematics, the preimage of an element `y` under a function `f` is the set of all `x` such that `f(x) = y`. It is the operation of inverting the function: going back from the output to the input.

In cryptography, this concept underlies the security of hash functions: preimage resistance requires that, given a hash `h`, it be computationally infeasible to find `m` such that `H(m) = h`. The function `H` acts as a one-way function: easy to compute, nearly impossible to invert.

On Bitcoin, this term comes up whenever hash functions are discussed, but it takes on a more specific meaning on Lightning, where the preimage designates the random secret value whose hash serves as a lock for payments. When a recipient issues an invoice, they generate a 32-byte *preimage*, compute its SHA-256 hash (the *payment hash*) and include it in the invoice. The HTLCs established along the payment route are locked by this hash. The payment is finalized only when the recipient reveals the *preimage* to the node preceding them on the route. That node can then unlock the corresponding HTLC, and the *preimage* propagates in the opposite direction, allowing each intermediate node to claim its funds. The revelation of the *preimage* thus constitutes the cryptographic proof that the payment was indeed received.

entries.title: PREMIUM
entries.body:
Additional amount paid above the standard or nominal price of an asset. In the context of Bitcoin, a premium can be observed in purchases, notably on exchange platforms, which can sometimes use this technique to make their margins on the brokerage service.

This notion of premium can also be found in peer-to-peer BTC purchases. Indeed, buying non-KYC bitcoins often comes with a premium over the standard market price, which can vary from 1% up to sometimes more than 10%. Several reasons explain this price difference. First, it is a common practice among P2P sellers that has become established over time. Second, sellers have fees associated with the transaction to send the funds to the buyer. There is also an increased risk of theft in P2P sales compared with transactions on regulated platforms, which justifies compensation for the risk taken. Finally, the extra cost may be linked to demand and to the quality of the exchange in terms of privacy. As a buyer, the privacy gain has a price that is reflected in the markup applied by the seller. Some bitcoiners also believe that the marked-up price of BTC bought P2P reflects its true price, and put forward the argument that the lower prices on regulated platforms are the result of a compromise on the privacy of your personal data.

entries.title: PREMIX
entries.body:
Intermediate account in the Whirlpool protocol that contains the UTXOs resulting from the Tx0 awaiting their first coinjoin cycle. The premix is a transitional state: UTXOs stay there until they are selected to participate in a coinjoin transaction.

Each UTXO in the premix account has exactly the nominal amount of the chosen pool (for example 0.01 BTC for the 0.01 pool), in addition to the mining fees needed for the first coinjoin cycle. These UTXOs are considered unmixed, because they are still directly traceable to the Tx0 that created them. They have not yet benefited from the link-breaking that coinjoin offers.

Once a premix UTXO is selected for a coinjoin cycle and the transaction is confirmed, it moves into the postmix account.

entries.title: PRIVATE CHANNEL
entries.body:
A Lightning channel that is not announced to the network and is therefore absent from the public node graph. Unlike a standard public channel, a private channel does not broadcast an announcement message (*channel announcement*) to other peers. It is invisible to third-party nodes and cannot be used to route payments for other users.

Private channels are the recommended channel type for nodes that do not route, such as nodes embedded in mobile devices. To receive a payment through a private channel, the existence of the channel and its parameters are revealed to the payer through *routing hints* embedded in the Lightning invoice.

The term “private” is somewhat misleading here: it simply means “unannounced”. On-chain heuristics, such as analysis of funding transactions or force closures, can allow an observer to infer the existence of these channels, as can analysis of payments to that node. It is in fact because of these channels that it is impossible to know the real size of the Lightning Network, since only public channels can be counted with certainty.

entries.title: PROBING
entries.body: A technique consisting of sending payments over the Lightning Network with no intention of completing them, in order to discover information about the network, notably the available routes and channel balances.

entries.title: PROOF OF RESERVES
entries.body:
Mechanism used by bitcoin exchange platforms to demonstrate that they do hold their customers' assets. The goal is to prove the company's solvency by verifying that its bitcoins are equal to or greater than the user balances that they are supposed to hold.

Platforms often use Merkle trees that include all of their users' balances. Each user can then verify that their balance is part of the total set, without revealing information about the other accounts. In parallel, the platform publicly signs the addresses that secure the bitcoins to prove that it controls them.

However, these methods have significant limitations, because proof of possession of the funds does not in itself prove the company's solvency. The exchange could, for example, secretly take on debts by contracting Lombard loans secured by the same bitcoins used in the proof of reserves. It could also display a balance of borrowed bitcoins while remaining insolvent. The problem with proof of reserves is that it focuses solely on verifying the platform's assets, without taking liabilities into account. 

Traditionally on Bitcoin, to celebrate the anniversary of the publication of the Genesis block, every January 3 is "*Proof-of-Keys Day*". Bitcoin holders are invited to all withdraw their funds from exchanges and store them in self-custody wallets, in order to test the solvency of these platforms.

But ultimately, if you truly want to protect yourself against the risk of exchange platforms going bankrupt, the only solution is to keep your bitcoins in self-custody.

entries.title: PROOF OF STAKE
entries.body:
A consensus mechanism that is an alternative to proof of work, in which validators are selected to propose and confirm blocks based on the quantity of tokens they lock up (“*stake*”) in the protocol. The more tokens a participant holds and locks up, the greater their probability of being chosen as a validator.

This mechanism is used by several cryptocurrency systems, notably Ethereum since its transition on September 15, 2022. Its proponents put forward a much lower energy consumption than that of proof of work. Its critics point out that it tends to concentrate validation power in the hands of the largest holders, reproducing a dynamic similar to that of traditional financial systems where wealth begets control in a fundamentally closed system, because it does not rely on a natural resource external to the protocol.

Bitcoin does not use proof of stake. Its protocol relies exclusively on proof of work, which ties the publication of a block to a real and verifiable energy expenditure, independent of the wealth accumulated by participants.

entries.title: PROOF-OF-KEY DAY
entries.body: An annual initiative observed every January 3 (the anniversary of the Genesis block) that encourages bitcoin holders to all withdraw their assets from exchange platforms at the same time and transfer them to *self-custody* solutions. The goal is to test the solvency of exchange platforms, by forcing them to prove that they do hold their users' bitcoins and that they are not engaging in fractional reserve. However, this practice is less and less followed today, which reduces its effectiveness. Ultimately, the best way to protect oneself against the bankruptcy of *exchanges* remains keeping one's bitcoins in *self-custody* all year round.

entries.title: PROP - PROPORTIONAL
entries.body: A method of calculating miner payouts in the context of mining pools. PROP simply distributes the block reward among miners in proportion to their contribution in *shares*. The counting of *shares* begins at the last block found by the pool and ends when a new block is found. Each new block resets the *share* counter to zero. This payout method directly reflects each miner's work.

entries.title: PROTON WALLET
entries.body: An open source Bitcoin wallet in *self-custody* developed by Proton, the Swiss company known for its privacy-focused services. Available as a web and mobile application, it is linked to a Proton account. Its distinctive feature is sending bitcoins via the recipient's email address: Proton automatically generates a fresh Bitcoin address associated with the recipient's wallet.

entries.title: PROXIMITY PREMIUM
entries.body:
In the context of Bitcoin mining, it refers to the financial advantage that miners obtain by reducing communication latency on the network. Miners located closer to one another receive new valid blocks more quickly, which allows them to stop wasting resources on a candidate block that sits on a branch with less accumulated work. This reduction in latency improves miners' returns, which naturally encourages them to cluster geographically in order to maximize their revenue.

The proximity premium is an inherent flaw in the way Bitcoin works, stemming from two mechanisms: the linearity of block ordering and the fact that the block reward is allocated exclusively to the miner who finds the block. This phenomenon therefore encourages the clustering of mining activities.

entries.title: PSAN
entries.body:
Acronym for “Prestataire de Services sur Actifs Numériques” (Digital Asset Service Provider). A French regulatory status introduced by the PACTE law of May 22, 2019, defining the legal framework applicable to companies that offer cryptocurrency-related services in France. The services concerned include the custody of digital assets, buying and selling against fiat currency, exchange between digital assets, and the operation of trading platforms.

Since 2019, mandatory registration with the AMF (Autorité des Marchés Financiers) has been required to carry out these activities in France. A more demanding optional license can also be obtained. Registration imposes obligations regarding anti-money laundering (AML/CFT) and identity verification (KYC).

With the entry into force of the European MiCA regulation (*Markets in Crypto-Assets*), the PSAN status is gradually being replaced by the harmonized European framework PSCA (Prestataire de Services sur Crypto-Actifs, or Crypto-Asset Service Provider), applicable in all member states of the European Union.

entries.title: PSBT
PSEUDO-RANDOM
entries.body:
This adjective is used to describe a sequence of numbers that, although the result of a deterministic process, displays characteristics approaching those of an ideal, truly random sequence. The notion of ideal randomness implies a total absence of predictability and of correlation between successive elements. A pseudo-random number is generated by a deterministic algorithm and therefore, in theory, it is entirely predictable if one knows the initial state of the generator.

A pseudo-random number generator (“*PRNG*” in English, or “GNPA” in French) is an algorithm used to produce such numbers. It generally starts from an initial value, or “seed”, and then applies a series of mathematical transformations to produce the sequence of numbers. Because of this determinism, it is important for cryptographic security that the initial seed remain secret. Pseudo-random sequences are widely used in various fields, notably cryptography, because they exhibit an apparently random behavior that is sufficient for many applications. Evaluating the quality of a PRNG rests on the extent to which its output approaches true randomness in terms of distribution, correlations and other statistical properties. In the context of Bitcoin, pseudo-random numbers are used to produce private keys, or to produce a seed for hierarchical deterministic wallets.

entries.title: PTLC
entries.body:
Conditional contracts intended to replace HTLCs (*Hash Time Locked Contracts*) for routing payments on the Lightning Network. A PTLC (*Point Time Locked Contract*) works on the same principle as an HTLC (locking funds that are released only if a cryptographic condition is satisfied) but uses elliptic curve points and signatures instead of hashes and preimages.

In an HTLC, all the hops of the same payment share the same hash. A spy node present on several hops can correlate the payments and identify that they belong to the same transaction. PTLCs eliminate this problem: each hop uses a different public key/signature pair, which makes payments untraceable from one hop to another.

The mechanism relies on *adaptor signatures*, a construction made practical by Schnorr signatures. The receiver provides a point (public key) to the payer. At each hop, a new secret is added through key aggregation, so that the revelation of the final signature compromises only the local secret, not the relationship between hops. If a PTLC is published on-chain, it appears as an ordinary Taproot spend, indistinguishable from a standard payment.

Beyond privacy, PTLCs reduce the block space used and open the way to new constructions such as *stuckless payments*, which make it possible to retry a stuck payment without risk of double payment. Their deployment requires changes to the Lightning protocol and relied on the availability of Schnorr signatures, activated with Taproot in 2021.

entries.title: PUBLIC CHANNEL
entries.body: A Lightning channel announced to the network via a *channel announcement* message broadcast to peers. Unlike a private channel, a public channel is included in the Lightning network graph: other nodes know of its existence, its capacity and its fee policies, which allows them to use it to route payments.

entries.title: PUBLIC POOL
entries.body:
An *open source* solo mining pool for Bitcoin, created by Benjamin Wilson. Unlike conventional pools that pool computing power and share rewards, Public Pool operates on the principle of *solo mining*: each miner individually attempts to find a block and, if successful, keeps the entire reward.

The platform charges no fees on its hosted instance. It provides a block *template* to miners, which saves them from having to run their own full node.

Public Pool is part of the *Open Source Miners United* ecosystem and integrates natively with projects such as the NerdMiner and the Bitaxe.

entries.title: PULL REQUEST
entries.body:
In the context of GitHub and other code hosting platforms, a *Pull Request* represents a request made by a contributor to merge their changes from one branch into another. It triggers a code review and a discussion before the changes are potentially merged (*merge*). This process is widely used in the development of Bitcoin node implementations, notably Bitcoin Core.

*The term “Pull Request” is often abbreviated by the acronym “PR”.*

entries.title: RELAY POLICY
ROUND PAYMENT
entries.body:
Internal chain analysis heuristic on Bitcoin that makes it possible to form a hypothesis about the nature of a transaction's outputs based on round amounts. In general, when faced with a simple payment *pattern* (1 or more inputs and 2 outputs), if one of the outputs spends a round amount, then it represents the payment. By elimination, if one output represents the payment, the other represents the change. It can therefore be inferred that it is likely that the user on the input side is still in possession of the output identified as the change.

It should be emphasized that this heuristic is not always applicable, since the majority of payments are still made in fiat units of account. Indeed, when a merchant in France accepts bitcoin, in general, they do not display stable prices in sats. They will rather opt for a conversion between the price in euros and the amount in bitcoins to be paid through their POS (such as BTCPay Server for example). There should therefore be no round number in the output of the transaction. Nevertheless, an analyst could attempt to perform this conversion by taking into account the exchange rate in effect when the transaction was broadcast on the network. If one day bitcoin becomes the preferred unit of account in our exchanges, this heuristic could become even more useful for analyses.

![Round payment: an input of 451,458 sats yields two outputs, including a round 200,000 sats (payment) and 248,607 (change).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/paiement-rond/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: SIMPLE PAYMENT
entries.body:
Transaction *pattern* (or model) used in chain analysis, characterized by the consumption of one or more UTXOs as inputs and the production of 2 UTXOs as outputs. This model will therefore look like this:

![Simple payment: an input of 50,000 sats produces two outputs, one to the recipient and the other returning as change.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/paiement-simple/assets/image-1.png)

This simple payment model indicates that we are likely in the presence of a sending or payment transaction. The user has consumed their own UTXO as inputs to satisfy, as outputs, a payment UTXO and a change UTXO (change returning to the same user). We therefore know that the observed user is likely no longer in possession of one of the two UTXOs in outputs (the payment one), but that they are still in possession of the other UTXO (the change one).

entries.title: STACK
entries.body:
In the context of the scripting language used to attach spending conditions to Bitcoin UTXOs, the stack is a "LIFO" (*Last In, First Out*) data structure used to store temporary elements during the execution of a script. Each operation in the script manipulates these stacks, where elements can be added (*push*) or removed (*pop*). Scripts use stacks to evaluate expressions, store temporary variables, and handle conditions.

In the execution of a Bitcoin script, 2 stacks can be used: the main stack and the alt (alternative) stack. The main stack is used for the majority of a script's operations. It is on this stack that script operations add, remove, or manipulate data. The alternative stack, for its part, is used to temporarily store data during the execution of the script. Certain specific opcodes, such as `OP_TOALTSTACK` and `OP_FROMALTSTACK`, make it possible to transfer elements from the main stack to the alternative stack and vice versa.

For example, when validating a transaction, the signatures and public keys are pushed onto the main stack and processed by successive opcodes to verify that the signatures match the keys and the transaction data.

entries.title: STALE - BLOCK
entries.body: Refers to a block with no child: a valid block, but one excluded from the main Bitcoin chain. It occurs when two miners find a valid block at the same chain height within a short span of time and broadcast it on the network. The nodes eventually choose a single block to include in the chain, according to the principle of the chain with the most accumulated work, making the other one "orphaned," "obsolete," or "stale."

entries.title: TIME PREFERENCE
entries.body:
Concept from Austrian economics that describes the tendency of individuals to prefer immediate satisfaction to future satisfaction. An individual with a high time preference favors present consumption; an individual with a low time preference agrees to defer their consumption in order to obtain a greater benefit in the future. This concept is central to the Austrian theory of interest and capital.

Time preference is directly linked to the quality of the money used. A money that loses its value over time (through inflation) encourages a high time preference: it is rational to spend quickly rather than to save. Conversely, a hard money, whose value is maintained or appreciates, encourages saving, long-term planning and productive investment.

Bitcoin, through its absolute scarcity and its disinflationary monetary policy, is often presented as a tool that promotes a low time preference. It would encourage its holders to adopt a long-term outlook, both in their financial choices and in their consumption behavior.

entries.title: TRANSACTION RELAY POLICY
entries.body:
Subset of relay policy that groups together all the rules applied by a Bitcoin node specifically for processing and relaying transactions on the peer-to-peer network. Transaction relay policy notably encompasses mempool policy and, by extension, standardness rules.

These rules determine whether a transaction received from a peer will be accepted, stored in the mempool, and then relayed to the other nodes on the network. They go beyond the mere format of individual transactions (covered by standardness rules) and also include considerations related to network management.

Like all policy rules, transaction relay policy is configured locally by each node and may vary from one node to another. It is distinct from relay policy in the broader sense, which also covers aspects not related to transactions, such as block handling or the management of connections with peers.

entries.title: WALLET
entries.body:
Software tool specifically designed to secure and manage a user's private keys. If the wallet is stored and managed on a software device that is itself installed on a general-purpose machine, it is called a "hot wallet". On the other hand, if it is stored in software that is itself installed on a hardware device dedicated solely to this task and not connected to the internet, it is called a "cold wallet". The wallet notably makes it possible to use private keys to sign transactions, and thus fulfill the conditions for spending bitcoins.

*In French, many people directly use the English term "wallet" to refer to a portefeuille.*
